analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare itself offer a drug plan that negotiates prescription prices directly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, it sat there until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the government, through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, to offer its own prescription drug plan to Medicare beneficiaries alongside private plans. The public plan would negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, use a scientifically assessed formulary to favor effective, lower-cost drugs, and include an appeals process for denied coverage, including outside review. Today Medicare is largely barred from negotiating drug prices, so this would create a government-run competitor to private insurers in the Medicare drug market.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, particularly those paying high out-of-pocket drug costs, would gain a lower-priced, nationally uniform public drug plan option that negotiates directly with manufacturers. Taxpayers also benefit to the extent that lower drug prices reduce Medicare's prescription drug subsidy costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans nationwide, giving beneficiaries a public alternative to private Part D plans.
Directs CMS to negotiate purchase prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers for drugs covered under the public plan — authority private plans exercise but Medicare itself lacks under current law.
Requires a formulary built on clinical evidence from AHRQ and an independent advisory committee, rewarding lower-cost, clinically effective drugs and encouraging generic substitution.
Creates an appeals process for denied benefits, including external review by an independent entity, and requires informing beneficiaries that the public plan exists.
Sets a uniform national premium for the public plan based on its actual per-capita cost, including administrative expenses.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue would fall as Medicare negotiated prices and steered use toward cheaper therapeutic equivalents and generics. Private Part D insurers would also face a government-run competitor for enrollment.

drawbacks.text: The public plan's formulary tools — tiered copays, prior authorization, step therapy, reference pricing — are the same utilization controls critics associate with private and government-run plans abroad, and some beneficiaries could face denial or delay of newer brand-name drugs.

Opponents of government price negotiation have long argued it could reduce manufacturers' returns and, over time, dampen investment in new drug development — a cost that would fall on future patients if it occurred.

A Medicare-operated plan would directly compete with private insurers and pharmacy benefit intermediaries that participate in Part D, concentrating more purchasing power and plan design authority in one federal agency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the upside is concrete: a nationwide public plan with negotiated prices, an evidence-based formulary, and appeal rights, at a premium pegged to actual cost. The main real tradeoff is that formulary incentives like step therapy and reference pricing could limit quick access to some newer brand-name drugs, and the long-run concern that heavy price negotiation could soften drug development incentives is a serious good-faith objection, though unproven. On balance the bill shifts bargaining power from manufacturers and private insurers toward patients and taxpayers, which is why it drew industry opposition and why it went nowhere in a Republican-controlled Senate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin and six colleagues introduced the bill on July 29, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that day.
No further action is recorded — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
All seven initial sponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. King; no Republican joined, and the Senate Finance Committee was chaired by a Republican whose panel controlled the bill's fate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and private Medicare drug insurers are better off: Medicare still cannot negotiate prices for a public plan, and the private Part D market they dominate was untouched.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six colleagues to cosponsor it on introduction.

for.name: Sens. Whitehouse, Reed, Brown, Baldwin, King, and Hirono
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only support it ever received.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action and no Republican cosponsors, it never advanced.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed letting Medicare negotiate drug prices, the core of this bill; the industry's opposition is a well-known feature of this recurring debate.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. King, no Republican cosponsor ever joined, and the bill died in a committee controlled by Republicans without a single recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill's core mechanism is Medicare negotiating purchase prices directly with manufacturers and steering use toward cheaper equivalents, which would cut the prices and revenue drug makers currently command in Part D. The industry's gain today is beneficiaries' and taxpayers' higher costs.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan offered nationwide would compete with private Part D plans for enrollment, threatening their role as the gatekeepers of the Medicare drug benefit. Their interest in preserving the private-only market runs against beneficiaries seeking lower prices.
Formulary incentives to substitute cheaper therapeutic equivalents and generics would shift volume toward generic manufacturers as brand-name drugs lose ground.
